Visualizing centrality, bootstrap and comparison results with the psychnets R package

Mohammed Saqr

University of Eastern Finland

Sonsoles López-Pernas

University of Eastern Finland
Source: vignettes/articles/visualizing-networks.Rmd
visualizing-networks.Rmd

A network diagram may show a striking pattern, but how can researchers tell which edges are precise and which nodes are comparatively important? For questionnaire constructs such as motivation and self-regulated learning, nodes denote measured characteristics and edges can represent associations adjusted for the other variables. This focuses attention on relations among constructs rather than on separate predictors or outcomes (Borsboom et al., 2021). A diagram provides a useful overview, yet node placement and edge thickness alone cannot establish estimation precision or comparative prominence. Visualising centrality, bootstrap and comparison results adds information needed to interpret those features with appropriate care (Jones et al., 2018).

In education, network methods have been used to examine how learning processes are connected. Studies have considered the relations among monitoring events and phases of regulation during collaborative learning (Malmberg et al., 2022), as well as the temporal and relational dynamics of self-regulation in academic writing (Saqr et al., 2021). Network approaches can therefore help researchers investigate how cognitive, motivational and regulatory processes co-occur or develop together, without assuming that an observed association demonstrates a causal effect. Saqr et al. (2024) discuss their use for analysing complex learning processes and the methodological choices involved.

Interpreting a fitted network requires more than identifying its visually prominent edges. Centrality measures summarise different aspects of a node’s position, but their rankings may depend on the measure used. Bootstrap intervals provide information about estimation uncertainty, difference tests assess contrasts between edges or nodes, and case-dropping procedures examine how centrality estimates respond to changes in the sample (Epskamp et al., 2018). When networks are estimated for two groups, permutation tests can assess differences in overall structure, global strength and individual edges (van Borkulo et al., 2023). Clear figures, paired with numerical results and careful reporting, help distinguish descriptive patterns from findings supported by uncertainty assessments (Burger et al., 2023).

This article demonstrates how to visualise and interpret these results using psychnets. It uses five self-regulated learning constructs from model-generated questionnaire responses to illustrate centrality bar and line plots, bootstrap intervals, difference matrices and forest plots, case-dropping stability curves, and network comparison plots. For each display, the emphasis is on what is plotted, how to read it, and what the observed results justify. The examples use the plot() method associated with each result object; the printed tables provide the values needed for reporting.

library(psychnets)

Data

SRL_GPT contains 300 sets of model-generated responses to the Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire. Each row contains construct scores on a scale from 1 to 7, rather than responses from an individual student. The GPT responses were produced for a study of how large language models answer psychological questionnaires (Vogelsmeier et al., 2025). The accompanying SRL_Claude data contain 300 responses generated by another model and are used for the two-group comparison. These data illustrate the methods; their associations should not be interpreted as evidence about a population of learners.

  • Nodes: CSU (cognitive strategy use), IV (intrinsic value), SE (self-efficacy), SR (self-regulation) and TA (test anxiety).
  • Observations: one row per generated response set; the data are complete.
head(SRL_GPT)
#>        CSU       IV       SE       SR   TA
#> 1 5.307692 5.666667 5.777778 5.333333 4.00
#> 2 5.846154 6.444444 6.000000 5.777778 4.00
#> 3 6.615385 6.666667 6.222222 6.333333 3.25
#> 4 5.692308 6.555556 6.333333 5.555556 4.50
#> 5 4.384615 5.555556 4.888889 4.777778 4.00
#> 6 4.846154 5.444444 5.666667 5.111111 3.50

ebic_glasso() fits the network used throughout the single-group examples. It estimates a Gaussian graphical model in which edges represent partial correlations, with regularisation selected using the extended Bayesian information criterion. An edge therefore describes a conditional association, not a causal relation.

fit <- ebic_glasso(SRL_GPT)
fit
#> <psychnet> glasso network
#>   nodes: 5   edges: 10   (undirected)
#>   lambda: 0.00861   gamma: 0.5
#>   optimality (KKT residual): 2.21e-10

The fitted network contains all 10 possible edges among the five constructs. The companion article on Gaussian graphical models discusses their interpretation; here the focus is on visualising the associated summaries and uncertainty estimates.

Which nodes are most central?

net_centralities() returns one row per node and a column for each requested measure. Strength adds the absolute values of a node’s edge weights, regardless of sign. Expected influence adds the signed weights, so positive and negative associations can offset each other. Betweenness describes the proportion of shortest paths between other nodes that pass through the node. These measures answer related but distinct questions, and none alone identifies a construct as a cause or an intervention target.

ct <- net_centralities(fit,
                       measures = c("strength", "expected_influence",
                                    "betweenness"))
ct
#>   node  strength expected_influence betweenness
#> 1  CSU 1.1984512         1.19845117   0.1666667
#> 2   IV 1.0012765         1.00127649   0.0000000
#> 3   SE 0.8492185         0.84921854   0.0000000
#> 4   SR 1.2314317         0.53172852   0.5000000
#> 5   TA 0.6082238        -0.09147935   0.0000000

Self-regulation has the largest strength (1.231) and betweenness (0.5), but its negative edge with test anxiety reduces its expected influence to 0.532, below that of cognitive strategy use (1.198), intrinsic value (1.001) and self-efficacy (0.849). Only cognitive strategy use and self-regulation lie on shortest paths between other nodes. plot() draws one panel per measure, with the nodes sorted by value so that the most central node is at the top:

plot(ct)

The ordering changes across panels. Self-regulation ranks first for strength and betweenness, but fourth for expected influence. Thus, a claim that a node is the most central is incomplete unless the measure is specified. The bar plots describe the observed values; they do not by themselves show whether differences in rank are statistically distinguishable.

Do the nodes keep their position across measures?

With type = "line", each node is traced across the measures while the nodes retain a common vertical ordering based on their mean standardised centrality. Each panel initially uses the scale of its own measure. Changes in a node’s position across panels make it easier to identify measures on which that node is relatively prominent or peripheral; the visual slope should not be treated as a numerical difference between measures with different units.

plot(ct, type = "line")

The scale argument determines how the values are displayed: "raw" (the default) retains the original values, "z" standardises each measure to a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1, and "relative" rescales each measure to the range 0 to 1. Standardisation makes differences in relative position easier to compare across the three measures, although it does not make the measures conceptually interchangeable.

plot(ct, type = "line", scale = "z")

Self-regulation changes position markedly: it is highest on strength and betweenness but much lower on expected influence. Test anxiety has the lowest strength and expected influence. These profiles help explain why the choice of centrality measure affects the substantive description of the same network.

How precise are the edges?

net_boot() repeatedly resamples rows from the data and re-estimates the network, retaining the resulting edge weights and centrality values. Their percentile bootstrap intervals summarise sampling uncertainty under this resampling procedure. More resamples are preferable for a substantive analysis, often at least 1,000; the example uses 250 to limit computation. Because these are model-generated response sets, the resampling units here are rows of generated data rather than human respondents.

set.seed(1)
bs <- net_boot(SRL_GPT, method = "glasso", n_boot = 250, cores = 1)
bs
#> <psychnet_bootstrap> glasso, 250 resamples, 95% CI
#>   10 edges (7 significant), 5 nodes, measures: strength, expected_influence

Seven of the 10 estimated edges have 95% bootstrap intervals that exclude zero. The default display places the observed edge weight beside its interval and sorts the edges by weight. Filled points and solid intervals identify those that exclude zero; open points and dashed intervals identify the others. Interval width indicates the precision of the estimate, while its position relative to zero shows whether that interval includes values of both signs.

plot(bs)

The intervals for the small positive associations between test anxiety and intrinsic value, self-efficacy, and cognitive strategy use include zero. By contrast, the negative association between self-regulation and test anxiety and the six positive associations among the other four learning constructs have intervals that exclude zero. This distinguishes uncertainty about individual edge weights from the mere presence of an edge in the fitted network.

How precise is each node’s centrality?

With type = "centrality", the plot displays the observed centrality estimates and their bootstrap intervals, in separate panels for strength and expected influence. It allows the reader to consider the uncertainty around each estimate rather than relying only on its position in the ranking.

plot(bs, type = "centrality")

as.data.frame(bs, what = "centrality")
#>   node  strength strength_lower strength_upper expected_influence
#> 1  CSU 1.1984512      1.0817999      1.3489871         1.19845117
#> 2   IV 1.0012765      0.8670417      1.1413809         1.00127649
#> 3   SE 0.8492185      0.7196350      1.0077951         0.84921854
#> 4   SR 1.2314317      1.0840409      1.3565767         0.53172852
#> 5   TA 0.6082238      0.3734560      0.7761419        -0.09147935
#>   expected_influence_lower expected_influence_upper
#> 1                1.0726933               1.34898708
#> 2                0.8670417               1.14138092
#> 3                0.7196350               1.00779507
#> 4                0.4018903               0.65431683
#> 5               -0.1648691              -0.02151559

The 95% strength intervals for cognitive strategy use (1.08 to 1.35) and self-regulation (1.08 to 1.36) overlap almost completely. Test anxiety has a lower observed strength, with an interval from 0.37 to 0.78. These displays suggest that the ordering of some nodes is uncertain, but overlap between separate intervals is not itself a formal test of a difference. The pairwise results below provide that assessment.

Which edges and nodes differ from one another?

With type = "edge_diff" or type = "centrality_diff", a matrix compares pairs of edges or centrality values. Items appear on both axes, ordered by their observed estimates, and the diagonal shows those estimates. The off-diagonal cells distinguish pairs with evidence of a difference from pairs without it: red indicates a larger estimate in the row, blue a smaller estimate, and faint cells indicate no detected difference. Stars indicate levels of statistical significance. Reading across a row helps identify which comparisons are supported, rather than treating the entire rank order as certain.

plot(bs, type = "edge_diff")

plot(bs, type = "centrality_diff", measure = "strength")

The strength matrix shows which observed differences between nodes are supported by the bootstrap comparisons. The corresponding difference_test() table reports each pair’s values, the observed difference, its interval, a p-value and a significant flag. It also provides the numerical evidence behind the coloured cells:

dt <- difference_test(bs, type = "strength")
dt
#>    item1 item2    value1    value2    obs_diff       lower       upper p_value
#> 1    CSU    IV 1.1984512 1.0012765  0.19717467 -0.01516075  0.43862886   0.080
#> 2    CSU    SE 1.1984512 0.8492185  0.34923263  0.12605796  0.63527516   0.000
#> 3     IV    SE 1.0012765 0.8492185  0.15205795 -0.09197932  0.36727209   0.208
#> 4    CSU    SR 1.1984512 1.2314317 -0.03298049 -0.21134715  0.18144546   0.712
#> 5     IV    SR 1.0012765 1.2314317 -0.23015517 -0.41550510 -0.04600301   0.024
#> 6     SE    SR 0.8492185 1.2314317 -0.38221312 -0.54711539 -0.20825524   0.000
#> 7    CSU    TA 1.1984512 0.6082238  0.59022738  0.38908973  0.79088205   0.000
#> 8     IV    TA 1.0012765 0.6082238  0.39305270  0.19311698  0.60820843   0.000
#> 9     SE    TA 0.8492185 0.6082238  0.24099475  0.02772224  0.47534139   0.016
#> 10    SR    TA 1.2314317 0.6082238  0.62320787  0.51502542  0.74080956   0.000
#>    significant
#> 1        FALSE
#> 2         TRUE
#> 3        FALSE
#> 4        FALSE
#> 5         TRUE
#> 6         TRUE
#> 7         TRUE
#> 8         TRUE
#> 9         TRUE
#> 10        TRUE

Seven of the 10 pairwise strength comparisons are flagged as significant. Test anxiety has lower strength than each of the other four nodes; self-regulation has higher strength than intrinsic value and self-efficacy; and cognitive strategy use has higher strength than self-efficacy. The remaining three comparisons are not significant: cognitive strategy use versus self-regulation (difference -0.033, p = 0.712), cognitive strategy use versus intrinsic value (p = 0.080), and intrinsic value versus self-efficacy (p = 0.208). The results support describing test anxiety as lowest in strength, but not identifying a uniquely highest-strength node.

Calling plot() on the difference-test table produces a matrix by default (style = "box"). This is useful for seeing which pairs show evidence of a difference at a glance.

plot(dt)

With style = "forest", each comparison appears on a separate row, showing the observed difference and its interval against a dashed reference line at zero. Comparisons whose intervals exclude zero are emphasised. Unlike the matrix, the forest plot also conveys the magnitude and direction of the observed differences, together with their uncertainty.

plot(dt, style = "forest")

Is the centrality order stable when cases are dropped?

net_stability() evaluates how centrality estimates change when progressively larger proportions of cases are omitted. For each subset, the network is re-estimated and its centrality values are correlated with those from the full data. The correlation-stability (CS) coefficient summarises the largest proportion of cases that can be dropped while a correlation of at least 0.7 is retained in at least 95% of the subsets. It assesses the robustness of centrality estimates to case deletion, not the precision of individual edges.

st <- net_stability(SRL_GPT, method = "glasso",
                    drop_prop = seq(0.1, 0.8, 0.1), iter = 25)
st
#> <psychnet_stability> glasso, 25 subsets/proportion
#>   CS-coefficient (pearson cor > 0.70 in > 95% of subsets):
#>     strength             0.80
#>     expected_influence   0.80

The reported CS-coefficient is 0.80 for both strength and expected influence, above the recommended value of 0.5 (Epskamp et al., 2018). This is the highest drop proportion examined here, so the result should not be extrapolated to larger omissions. The plot shows the proportion dropped on the horizontal axis and the mean correlation with the full-sample centrality values on the vertical axis. Each measure has a line with a band representing one standard deviation, alongside a dashed threshold. Correlations that remain high as more rows are removed indicate comparatively stable centrality estimates in this example; the calculation uses only 25 subsets per proportion.

plot(st)

Do the networks of two groups differ?

net_compare() implements a permutation-based network comparison test (van Borkulo et al., 2023). The procedure repeatedly shuffles group membership and re-estimates the two networks, providing reference distributions for the observed group differences. The network structure statistic, M, is the largest absolute difference between corresponding edge weights. The global strength statistic, S, measures the absolute difference between the groups’ sums of absolute edge weights. The procedure also tests individual edges. Here the groups comprise GPT-generated and Claude-generated responses, not samples of students.

cmp <- net_compare(SRL_GPT, SRL_Claude, iter = 250)
summary(cmp)
#>                test statistic observed     p_value significant
#> 1 network structure         M 0.562165 0.003984064        TRUE
#> 2   global strength         S 1.092696 0.003984064        TRUE

Both global tests are significant at the conventional 0.05 level (p = 0.004 for both). The largest absolute edge difference is 0.562. The sum of absolute edge weights is 1.093 greater in the Claude-response network (3.537 versus 2.444). The default plot shows the permutation distribution of S, with the observed statistic indicated and its p-value in the title. An observed value well into the tail suggests that the group difference is unusual under random reassignment.

plot(cmp)

The observed global strength difference is approximately 1.09, to the right of the displayed permutation distribution, whose upper end is around 0.6. This visualises the small permutation p-value; it does not identify which edges account for the difference.

With type = "structure", the same display is produced for M, the largest absolute edge difference. It assesses whether the most pronounced edge-level discrepancy is unusually large under permutation.

plot(cmp, type = "structure")

With type = "edges", a bar represents the observed absolute difference for each corresponding edge. Colour indicates whether the edge comparison is significant at alpha, and the title reports how many edges meet that criterion. The plot therefore complements the two global tests with a view of where the differences occur.

plot(cmp, type = "edges")

The underlying table gives the weight of each edge in both networks, the absolute difference, its permutation p-value and the significance indicator:

as.data.frame(cmp)
#>    from to    weight_1     weight_2 difference     p_value       p_raw
#> 1   CSU IV  0.41166866  0.001744267 0.40992440 0.003984064 0.003984064
#> 2   CSU SE  0.38290223  0.223973564 0.15892867 0.007968127 0.007968127
#> 3    IV SE  0.15992605 -0.402239002 0.56216505 0.003984064 0.003984064
#> 4   CSU SR  0.35481359  0.728177591 0.37336401 0.003984064 0.003984064
#> 5    IV SR  0.31909443  0.574170376 0.25507595 0.003984064 0.003984064
#> 6    SE SR  0.20767208  0.221496430 0.01382435 0.884462151 0.884462151
#> 7   CSU TA  0.04906668  0.525584044 0.47651736 0.003984064 0.003984064
#> 8    IV TA  0.11058735 -0.013854928 0.12444228 0.131474104 0.131474104
#> 9    SE TA  0.09871818 -0.417575459 0.51629364 0.003984064 0.003984064
#> 10   SR TA -0.34985157 -0.428181457 0.07832989 0.350597610 0.350597610
#>    significant
#> 1         TRUE
#> 2         TRUE
#> 3         TRUE
#> 4         TRUE
#> 5         TRUE
#> 6        FALSE
#> 7         TRUE
#> 8        FALSE
#> 9         TRUE
#> 10       FALSE

Seven of the 10 individual edge comparisons are significant. The three largest absolute differences are IV–SE (0.160 in GPT versus -0.402 in Claude), SE–TA (0.099 versus -0.418) and CSU–TA (0.049 versus 0.526). The first two change sign, whereas the third remains positive but is substantially larger in the Claude-response network. The comparisons indicate different patterns in these generated response sets, not necessarily differences between human learner populations.

Summary of the plot methods

Result (verb) plot() options Question
net_centralities() type = "bar" / "line"; scale = "raw" / "z" / "relative" Which nodes are central, on which measure?
net_boot() type = "edges" / "centrality" / "edge_diff" / "centrality_diff" / "predictability" How precise are edges and centralities, and which differ?
difference_test() style = "box" / "forest" Which pairs differ, and by how much?
net_stability() one figure Is the centrality order stable when cases are dropped?
net_compare() type = "strength" / "structure" / "edges" Do two networks differ?

Each display should be interpreted alongside its underlying numerical results, obtained from the corresponding result object or as.data.frame(). In particular, observed rankings should be distinguished from tested pairwise differences, and global group differences from edge-specific findings. The network itself can be drawn with plot(fit), which uses the cograph package and is covered in the article Visualizing networks with cograph.
